title: Insulating a cold-water storage tank
subtitle: Fit foam slab insulation around the sides, ends, and lid of a loft cold-water storage tank to prevent freezing in cold weather
excerpt: How to insulate a cold-water storage tank in a loft. Covers measuring the tank, cutting foam slabs to fit each face, securing the insulation, and fitting an insulated lid, while leaving the tank base uninsulated.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade plumbing practice and Water Regulations Advisory Scheme guidance on tank insulation (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: A plastic, fibreglass, or galvanised steel water storage tank typically sited in the loft that stores cold water for the domestic plumbing system. It is fed from the mains supply via a ball valve and supplies the hot water cylinder and sometimes the cold taps. Volume is commonly 190 to 230 litres.

Pre-cut foam panels or a purpose-made fibreglass jacket designed to wrap a standard-size water tank. Custom-cut from 25 to 50 mm closed-cell foam board for non-standard tanks. The insulation must cover the sides, ends, and top but NOT the base: any warmth rising from the building below should be allowed to reach the base of the tank.

takes an hour and requires no plumbing work. BEGINNER: measure, cut foam, and tape in place.
Measure the tank and cut the foam slabs

Measure the height, length, and width of each face of the tank. Use 50 mm thick closed-cell foam board for loft tanks. Cut each foam slab slightly oversize and trim to a close fit with the utility knife guided along a straight batten. For circular tanks, cut the foam in strips that wrap around the circumference in sections.
Fit the side and end panels

Press the foam slabs against each face of the tank in turn. Hold them in place with broad adhesive tape wrapped around the tank at top and bottom, or use a purpose-made tank jacket's straps. Cut holes in the foam where pipes enter and exit the tank sides, keeping the holes a close fit around the pipes.
Fit the lid but leave the base bare

Cut a foam slab for the lid, fitting it so the lid can still be lifted for inspection. Do NOT insulate the base of the tank. Warmth from the building structure below the loft floor rises into the loft void and provides a small but useful heat source at the tank base. Insulating the base seals this off, which can actually increase the risk of freezing in extreme cold.
Insulate the overflow and vent pipes

Lag the pipework running from the tank for at least 600 mm in each direction from the tank body using foam pipe lagging cut to length with the utility knife. Pipes entering through the eaves or roof space are the most vulnerable to freezing: focus on these runs first.

attrs.symptom: Foam slabs will not stay in place against the tank sides
attrs.cause: The adhesive tape has not bonded to the foam or tank surface due to dust or moisture.
attrs.fix: Wipe the tank surface with a dry cloth before taping. Use self-adhesive foam tape or a belt of strapping tape under tension around the full perimeter of the tank.

attrs.symptom: Tank freezes despite the jacket being fitted
attrs.cause: Cold air flows through the loft directly onto the tank from an unsealed eaves gap, or the foam thickness is insufficient for the local climate.
attrs.fix: Block draughts at the eaves near the tank with loft insulation batt. Increase the foam thickness to 100 mm on the most exposed sides.
